title: Is the US Warming Hole a Moist‐Enthalpy Hole? Soil‐Moisture Trends Organize Dry and Moist Heat Across CONUS
content:
Abstract

The United States (US) summer warming hole, marked by muted warming or cooling in maximum dry-bulb temperature (T max) across parts of the central and southeastern US, is a regional exception to broader warming. However, T max does not capture atmospheric total heat content when humidity changes simultaneously. Using ERA5 reanalysis from 1950 to 2020, we examine summer trends in T max, maximum wet-bulb temperature (T w,max), and maximum equivalent temperature (T e,max) across the contiguous US (CONUS). The dry-bulb warming hole strengthens from June to August, yet humidity-sensitive metrics show sustained increases across many of the same areas. Decomposing T e into temperature and humidity contributions shows that rising specific humidity offsets or exceeds weak or negative T max trends throughout much of the warming hole region. In the moistening core of the region, a latent heat contribution of order +0.5°C decade−1 accompanies near-zero dry-bulb trends. This opposition between sensible and latent contributions makes the warming hole fundamentally metric-dependent. Moist-heat amplification co-occurs with wetting soil moisture, rising latent heat flux, and shallower boundary layers, whereas the most strongly drying regions show boundary-layer deepening and a negative humidity contribution. The US warming hole thus reflects a shift in heat exposure from sensible toward latent forms, linking regional heat-risk assessment to humidity, soil moisture, and boundary-layer processes.
